podcast.body: "Sunday Bloody Sunday" from the spring of 1983 tells the story of the Bloody Sunday incident in Derry, Northern Ireland on January 30, 1972, when British soldiers opened fire on a protest march, shooting 26 unarmed people and killing 14, some while trying to help the wounded. The troubles had begun in the late 1960s, with violence between those loyal to the British monarchy and Republicans who wanted the North to join the Republic of Ireland. When Bono wrote the song, the troubles were still very much ongoing — peace was not declared until 1998 with the Good Friday Agreement, after more than 3,500 people had been killed. "That's an incident, the most famous incident in Northern Ireland. And it's the strongest way of saying, how long?"

podcast.body: While often associated with the Bloody Sunday massacre in Derry, Northern Ireland on January 30, 1972, the song is primarily about U2's internal conflict and dilemma during the 1982 St. Patrick's Day Parade in New York City. The band had been booked to march in the parade, which manager Paul McGinnis secured as a good gimmick for the Irish band, but they discovered that members of the IRA would also be participating. U2, being against the fighting extending beyond Ireland, decided not to march, leading to a confrontation between McGinnis and some IRA members. The song's sentiment questions the longevity of such hatred. "It's not actually about what happened in Dairy on January 30, 1972. It's really more about the dilemma and the conflict U-2 had during the 1982 St. Patrick's Day Parade in New York City."
